description: October-November observation bank. Archival photographs and regional examples, not live sightings.

cards.title: Leaves underfoot
cards.alt: Red, orange, yellow and pale fallen leaves lie on green grass.
cards.creator: waferboard
cards.notes: Source date field says 1 October 2018; filename begins 181020. Day is uncertain.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Compare colour, edges and decay in fallen leaves.
cards.notice: Describe two differences between the leaves. What can you point to?
cards.explain: Does this photograph prove when the leaves fell? What more would you need to know?
cards.returnPrompt: Choose one patch near school. Record its date and leaf cover, then return to the same spot.
cards.teacherNote: A photograph records one place and moment. Colour alone does not establish the date or cause of change. Compare repeated observations rather than assuming a fixed autumn timetable.

cards.title: A leaf worth looking at
cards.alt: A large yellow bigleaf maple leaf lies on a woodland path, showing pointed lobes and branching veins.
cards.creator: Thayne Tuason
cards.location: Devil’s Gulch Trail, Chelan County, Washington, USA
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: A large fallen leaf offers evidence of shape, veins and autumn colour.
cards.photoTitle: A bigleaf maple leaf in autumn
cards.notice: Follow the leaf edge with your eyes or a description. What shapes repeat?
cards.explain: Which features would help you compare this leaf with another? Which details are missing?
cards.returnPrompt: Look for a fallen leaf without picking living leaves. Sketch its outline and compare with a tree guide.
cards.teacherNote: Use the image source identification and the BC Tree Book together. Bigleaf maple has deeply cut lobes; colour by itself is not enough to identify a tree.

cards.title: Patterns in a cone
cards.alt: A brown Douglas-fir cone hangs among green needles, with pointed bracts projecting between its scales.
cards.creator: RVWithTito
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Compare the structure of a cone and the needles around it.
cards.notice: Find one repeated shape and one detail that stands out.
cards.explain: How could a close view help us check which kind of cone this is?
cards.returnPrompt: Observe a cone where it lies. Describe it before looking at a labelled tree guide.
cards.teacherNote: The BC Tree Book describes three-pronged bracts on Douglas-fir cones. A cone on the ground does not prove it came from the nearest tree. Leave habitat materials in place.

cards.title: Life on fallen wood
cards.alt: Several tan mushrooms grow in an overlapping cluster on dark wood, surrounded by ferns.
cards.creator: Gerry Thomasen
cards.location: Near Long Beach, Vancouver Island, British Columbia, Canada
cards.notes: Species is uncertain: source calls these “Honey Mushrooms?” Do not present a firm species identification.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: A cluster of mushrooms shows how fungi can grow on woody material.
cards.notice: Describe where the mushrooms are growing. Avoid guessing their names.
cards.explain: What questions could this image help us ask about the wood? What can it not prove?
cards.returnPrompt: From a path, compare damp and dry-looking wood. Record what is visible without touching fungi.
cards.teacherNote: Many fungi produce visible fruiting bodies, including in autumn. A single photograph cannot establish edibility or the whole decomposition process. Never taste or pick unknown fungi.

cards.title: A tiny landscape
cards.alt: A bright green carpet of moss follows the rounded surface of a fallen log.
cards.creator: Lumpytrout
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Observe the texture and growing surface of a moss carpet.
cards.notice: Zoom in. Describe the shapes and the surface supporting them.
cards.explain: How is this surface similar to, or different from, the ground nearby?
cards.returnPrompt: Compare two small surfaces from an accessible observation point. Record where moss is visible.
cards.teacherNote: Mosses are small non-vascular plants. Describe the image without inventing a species identification or measuring moisture by appearance alone. Do not scrape samples.

cards.title: Moss or something else?
cards.alt: Grey-green lobes of shield lichen spread over rough bark.
cards.creator: Randal (rambryum)
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Compare lichen lobes and the bark surface beneath them.
cards.notice: Describe the edge, colour and texture you can see or learn from the image description.
cards.explain: Compare this with the moss photograph. What evidence supports a difference?
cards.returnPrompt: Look at a tree or rock from a path. Record a shape and a question; leave it attached.
cards.teacherNote: Lichens involve fungi and photosynthetic partners; they are not moss. One lichen sighting is not a stand-alone measure of air quality. The image source names this lichen; local look-alikes need checking.

cards.title: Weather over the coast
cards.alt: Low clouds hang over a waterfront city and an evergreen-covered slope at Stanley Park.
cards.creator: Thorfinn Stainforth
cards.location: Stanley Park, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: A rainy archival view provides clues about water, cloud and visibility.
cards.notice: Describe the sky, distant land and water. What is visible and what is hard to see?
cards.explain: What could happen to rain on a roof, soil or pavement? Which idea could we check?
cards.returnPrompt: After rain, observe from a safe dry place. Sketch where water collects and where it may move next.
cards.teacherNote: A cloudy or misty view does not by itself prove rain is falling. Use the source description, then predict possible runoff near school. One still image does not measure flow speed or water quality.

cards.title: A stream close to home
cards.alt: Shallow water flows between rounded rocks beneath dense forest vegetation in Tynehead Regional Park.
cards.creator: waferboard
cards.location: Tynehead Regional Park, Surrey, British Columbia, Canada
cards.notes: Source date field says 1 August 2014; image identifier is 140810-13. Day is uncertain.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: A Surrey stream photograph supports questions about flow, shade and streamside habitat.
cards.notice: Describe two features beside or within the stream.
cards.explain: How might water arriving from nearby streets affect this place? What evidence would we need?
cards.returnPrompt: From school grounds, map a possible route for rainwater. Mark guesses with a question mark.
cards.teacherNote: This is an archival Surrey image, not a current site report. Surrey explains that pollutants entering storm drains can reach waterways. Stay on designated viewing areas; do not enter streams.

cards.title: Salmon: look for evidence
cards.alt: A group of red sockeye salmon is visible in shallow river water.
cards.creator: Theinterior
cards.notes: Source description dates the photograph to 8 October 2010; embedded camera date is 10 October 2006. Exact capture date is uncertain. Not evidence of salmon present in Surrey today.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: An archived BC salmon image supports discussion of fish, streams and seasonal movement.
cards.photoTitle: Sockeye salmon in the Adams River
cards.notice: What can you observe about the fish and its surroundings?
cards.explain: Can one photograph prove that a fish is spawning? What evidence or source would help?
cards.returnPrompt: Compare this dated salmon image with a current official Surrey viewing update or a supervised observation.
cards.teacherNote: Surrey lists autumn salmon viewing opportunities, but dates and sightings vary by site, species and year. This historical photo does not confirm a run today. Never disturb fish or enter the stream.

cards.title: A gathering of birds
cards.alt: A dense flock of white and dark-winged snow geese rises into the air.
cards.creator: ShayneKayePhoto
cards.location: George C. Reifel Migratory Bird Sanctuary, Westham Island, Delta, British Columbia, Canada
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Observe a flock of snow geese and ask what evidence could reveal seasonal movement.
cards.notice: Describe the birds and their spacing. Which actions can you actually see?
cards.explain: What would repeated observations tell us that this single photograph cannot?
cards.returnPrompt: Watch birds from a distance near school. Record number, place and visible behaviour without feeding them.
cards.teacherNote: The photograph is from Reifel in Delta. It is a regional example, not proof of birds at school. Do not infer that every bird seen in autumn is migrating or that a pose reveals its intention.

cards.title: A web holds clues
cards.alt: A large dew-covered spiderweb stretches between a tree trunk and surrounding vegetation.
cards.creator: GabrielleMerk
cards.location: UNKNOWN — location not documented on source page
cards.notes: Source describes dew drops from early morning fog. Location is unknown; use as a general comparison image.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Look for repeating patterns where tiny water drops collect on a web.
cards.notice: Trace or describe a repeating pattern. Where are the droplets?
cards.explain: Could the photograph alone tell us how the droplets formed? Explain what is uncertain.
cards.returnPrompt: Look for a web without touching it. Compare its pattern with the photograph or a verbal description.
cards.teacherNote: Use “web with droplets” in student observations. Even when a source calls droplets dew, the visual evidence alone may not distinguish condensation from rain. Webs are not exclusive to autumn.

cards.title: A fallen tree, a living place
cards.alt: A huge moss-covered nurse log spans a forest, with trees above and a person below for scale.
cards.creator: Ademoor
cards.location: Carmanah Walbran Provincial Park, British Columbia, Canada
cards.notes: Commons version was cropped 1% horizontally by Sebastian Wallroth in December 2023 to remove a border; this bank preserves that published frame.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Compare the scale of a nurse log, trees and a person in a coastal forest.
cards.notice: Find evidence of plants growing on or near the fallen wood.
cards.explain: Why might this fallen tree matter to other living things? Separate an idea from visible evidence.
cards.returnPrompt: Observe fallen wood from a path. Draw a relationship and label it “observed” or “possible”.
cards.teacherNote: Down wood can provide habitat and support plant growth. Do not lift logs to find organisms. An observation can suggest a relationship without proving every cause.

cards.title: Small life among leaves
cards.sourceTitle: Pacific sideband Snail in Leaf litter - Flickr - brewbooks.jpg
cards.alt: A Pacific sideband snail rests among fallen leaves and twigs, with a finger nearby for scale.
cards.creator: brewbooks
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Leaf litter provides a setting for observing a small animal and its surroundings.
cards.notice: Describe the animal and one feature of its surroundings.
cards.explain: What might this place provide? Which part is visible, and which part is an inference?
cards.returnPrompt: Study leaf litter in place from a safe observation point. Record one detail without collecting animals.
cards.teacherNote: This photo is an example of leaf-litter habitat. Do not assume the same snail species occurs locally. Leave animals and shelter undisturbed; no touching or collecting is needed.

cards.title: Shapes that repeat
cards.sourceTitle: Ferns Capilano Park Vancouver British Columbia Canada 01.jpg
cards.alt: Green fern fronds spread from a shaded rocky shelf in a forest.
cards.creator: RestfulC401 / WinterforceMedia
cards.location: Capilano River Regional Park, North Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
cards.notes: The source description says ferns and Commons categorizes the image as Polystichum munitum; use cautious caption “ferns” if exact species is not needed.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Ferns offer leaf shapes and growing conditions to compare with nearby plants.
cards.photoTitle: Ferns on a forest rock shelf
cards.notice: Describe a repeating shape along the frond.
cards.explain: Which comparisons would help distinguish this fern from a tree branch or moss?
cards.returnPrompt: Compare two plants from the same observation point. Use shapes and arrangement rather than size alone.
cards.teacherNote: Use the source label for the photographed plant. The task is evidence-based comparison, not unverified local identification. Seasonal change can be subtle in plants that remain green.

cards.title: Many kinds of green
cards.alt: Broad maple leaves and tall conifer trees share a green forest canopy.
cards.creator: Arnold C
cards.location: Capilano River Regional Park, North Vancouver District, British Columbia, Canada
cards.notes: Source identifies Tsuga heterophylla and Acer macrophyllum. Copyright holder permits any use with proper attribution, including redistribution, derivative and commercial use. This is an evergreen/deciduous comparison, photographed in spring.
cards.context: Archival reference image; not a current Surrey observation.
cards.changes: Resized and converted to WebP; full frame preserved.
cards.topic: Compare broadleaf and conifer trees using a spring reference photograph.
cards.notice: Find two contrasting shapes or colours in the forest view.
cards.explain: Which trees might change differently through the year? How could we investigate?
cards.returnPrompt: Choose one repeatable viewpoint near school. Sketch or photograph it with school equipment on two dates.
cards.teacherNote: Different plants change in different ways. A broad forest photograph cannot reliably identify every tree. Record dates, viewpoint and conditions before comparing images.
